1. A Continent of Kingdoms
2. Why Europe Came
3. The Meeting in Berlin
4. Lines Drawn on a Map
5. Taking the Land
6. The People Who Said No
7. What the Scramble Left Behind

conference: a big meeting where important decisions are made
territory: an area of land that a country controls
protectorate: a land controlled and "protected" by a stronger country
treaty: a written agreement between rulers or countries
resistance: fighting back against something unfair
independence: being free to rule yourself
amalgamation: joining separate things together into one

Long before this story begins, Africa was not empty and it was not waiting. It was full of kingdoms, cities and busy markets, some of them older than most countries in Europe. If you had walked across it two hundred years ago, you would have passed traders, teachers, farmers and kings, each in a land they knew as home.

image.note: Bustling West African market city, mudbrick-and-plaster architecture, traders with cloth and brass, scholars with books; prosperous and ordered

pages.text: In the north, the Sokoto Caliphate stretched across what is now northern Nigeria, with libraries in Kano and scholars who wrote in Arabic. In the forest to the south stood the Kingdom of Benin, famous for bronze work so fine that people still travel across the world to see it. These were not small places. They were powerful states with armies, laws and long histories.

image.note: Split scene: a Kano scholar with manuscripts; a Benin bronze plaque being cast; reverent, detailed

pages.text: Across the whole continent it was the same. The Asante kingdom traded in gold. Ethiopia had been a Christian empire for more than a thousand years. Buganda, Zulu, Kongo, and hundreds of other peoples governed themselves, spoke their own languages, and traded with one another and with the wider world. Africa knew exactly who it was.

image.note: A simple, warm map dotted with named kingdoms across the continent, each marked with a small icon of its craft or trade

pages.text: So why did the ships come? The answer began far away, in the factories of Europe. New machines could spin cloth and make steel faster than ever before, but the machines were hungry. They needed rubber, palm oil, cotton, copper and tin, and much of it grew or lay buried in Africa.

image.note: A smoky European factory interior, huge machines, raw materials stacked at the door; the hunger made visible

pages.text: There was a second reason, and it was pride. The countries of Europe, Britain, France, Germany, Belgium, Portugal and others, were rivals. Each one wanted to be the biggest and the richest. If France took land in Africa, Britain wanted more, and so on, like children grabbing at sweets so that no one else could have them.

image.note: Cartographic image of European flags planted along the African coastline, each reaching inland; tone wary, not comic

pages.text: The Europeans told themselves a story to make it feel right. They said they were bringing help and progress to people who needed it. But Africa had its own kings, its own schools and its own trade. It did not need to be taken over. The real reasons were money and rivalry, dressed up in kinder words.

image.note: A European official in a pith helmet gesturing grandly; behind him, an African elder watching, calm and unconvinced; dignity with the elder

pages.text: In the winter of 1884, important men from fourteen countries gathered in the city of Berlin, in Germany. They sat around a long table, with a great map of Africa pinned to the wall, and they began to talk about how the continent should be shared out between them.

image.note: The conference room: long table, gas lamps, a wall map of Africa, formally dressed men; historical, sober

pages.text: Look carefully at that room, because something is missing from it. Not one African was invited. Not one king, not one trader, not one person from any of the lands on that map was asked what they wanted. The people whose homes were being divided were not even in the building.

image.note: Same room, but the empty chair at the head is emphasised; the map of Africa looms large; the absence is the point

pages.text: The meeting went on for months. When it ended, the men had agreed on rules for claiming African land. If a European country could show it "controlled" a place, the others would let it keep it. It was, in truth, a set of rules for a race. History remembers that race by a simple name: the Scramble for Africa.

image.note: Hands signing a document; the map now marked with early dividing lines; weighty

pages.text: Now the race began in earnest. Back in Africa, agents of the European countries hurried inland to claim as much as they could. They drew borders with rulers and pens, straight lines across deserts, forests and rivers they had never even seen.

image.note: A hand drawing a hard straight line across a detailed map, cutting through a river and a settlement; uncomfortable

pages.text: Because the mapmakers did not know the land, those lines did terrible things. A single family could wake up to find a border ran between their house and their farm. People who had always been one nation were split in two. Peoples who had long been rivals were pushed together into the same new colony and told they were now one.

image.note: A village with a dotted border line cutting straight through it; a family on either side; human, quiet

pages.text: This is why, even today, the map of Africa has so many straight borders. Rivers and mountains make wavy, natural lines. Straight lines are made by rulers on a table far away. Every straight border you see is a mark left by the Scramble.

image.note: Modern political map of Africa with the straight borders subtly highlighted; clear, informative

pages.text: Claiming land on a map was one thing. Taking it in real life was another. Sometimes the Europeans used paper. Traders and officials would ask a local ruler to sign a treaty, often written in a language the ruler could not read. The ruler might think he was agreeing to trade. In fact, the paper said he had given his kingdom away.

image.note: A chief presented with a document by a trading-company agent; interpreter beside them; tension beneath politeness

pages.text: In what is now Nigeria, a trading business called the Royal Niger Company gathered many such treaties along the great river. Piece by piece, papers and promises were turned into ownership, and a company came to claim lands that had belonged to kingdoms for centuries.

image.note: A riverboat flying a company flag on the Niger; palm-oil barrels; a stone marker on the bank; historical, specific

pages.text: When paper did not work, there was force. The European armies had a new weapon, the machine gun, which could fire faster than any army had ever fired before. African soldiers were often brave and skilled, but courage alone could not always stand against such weapons. Many kingdoms that had ruled for hundreds of years fell in only a few years.

image.note: NOT graphic: a lone brass war horn and a fallen royal standard on empty ground at dusk; loss shown through objects, not bodies

pages.text: But Africa did not simply hand itself over, and this part of the story matters most of all. Everywhere the Europeans went, people resisted. They fought, they refused, they hid, and they outwitted. The Scramble was never quiet, and it was never easy for those who came to take.

image.note: A determined line of African defenders on a ridge at dawn, banners raised; proud, not defeated

pages.text: In West Africa, a leader named Samori Ture built an army and held off the French for many years, moving his people rather than surrender. In the forests near the River Niger, the Ekumeku fighters slipped through the trees and struck again and again, so that the British could never feel safe. Resistance had many faces and many names.

image.note: Two vignettes: a mounted West African commander; forest fighters melting between trees; heroic, human

pages.text: And in one place, resistance won completely. When Italy tried to take Ethiopia, the Ethiopian emperor gathered a great army. At a place called Adwa, in 1896, they defeated the Italians so soundly that Ethiopia stayed free. While nearly all of Africa was taken, Ethiopia kept its independence, and the whole continent remembered it.

image.note: The Ethiopian standard raised on a highland after Adwa; drums and banners; triumphant, dignified

pages.text: These stories are often left out of the history books written far away. But they are true, and they are yours. The people of Africa were never only something that was done to. They were people who chose, who fought, and who never fully agreed to be ruled.

image.note: An elder telling this to gathered children under a tree at dusk; the children rapt; warm, connecting past to present

pages.text: By about the year 1914, the race was over. Almost the whole of Africa had been divided among a handful of European countries. Only Ethiopia and Liberia remained fully independent. A continent of hundreds of nations had been packed into a few dozen colonies, with borders drawn by strangers.

image.note: 1914 colonial map of Africa, colour-blocked by European power, Ethiopia and Liberia standing out; sobering, clear

pages.text: Nigeria itself was made this way. In 1914, the British joined a northern protectorate and a southern one together and called the whole thing Nigeria. Hundreds of peoples, with different languages, faiths and histories, found themselves inside one border they had never chosen. That is how a country can be made by other people's hands.

image.note: The 1914 map of Nigeria, north and south being joined; small icons of its many peoples along the edges

pages.text: Those borders did not disappear when the Europeans finally left. The countries of Africa today, including Nigeria, still live inside the lines drawn at that table in Berlin. Some of the difficulties of modern Africa, and some of its remarkable mixtures too, began in the Scramble.

image.note: Modern Nigeria on a map, busy and alive: a city skyline rising from the old outline; present-day, hopeful

pages.text: So why learn all this? Because you cannot understand your own country without it. The Scramble for Africa was unfair, and it was painful, but knowing the true story is a kind of strength. The people who resisted did not give up hope, and neither should you. Africa's story did not end at that table. It is still being written, and now it is being written by Africans.

image.note: A modern Nigerian child closing this very book on a sunny estate step, looking up and out; full circle, forward-looking
